name: Rear Delt Fly

claims.text: Set the machine's handles to the reverse-fly position and sit facing the machine with the chest pressed against the pad.

quotes.text: Adjust the handles of the pec deck machine in the reverse fly setting.
Sit facing the machine with chest pressed against the pad and handles adjusted to shoulder height.

claims.text: Adjust the chest pad and handles so you grip the handles at shoulder height, arms reaching forward.

quotes.text: Adjust the chest support and handles so that you can grip the handles at shoulder height and get a long range of motion.
Extend your arms straight in front of you and grab the handles with an overhand or neutral grip at shoulder height.

claims.text: Keep a slight bend in the elbows throughout: the arms shouldn't be straight, and the elbows shouldn't bend much either (Motra lists bending the elbows too much as a common mistake). A neutral or overhand grip is used.

quotes.text: Maintain a slight bend in your elbows throughout the movement for an optimal rear delt engagement. Your arms shouldn’t be extended straight. On the other hand, don’t bend your elbows too much while performing this exercise.
Grasp the handles with a neutral or overhand grip, keeping elbows slightly bent.
Bending elbows too much

claims.text: Pull the handles back in a wide arc, bringing the arms out to the sides, then return slowly.

quotes.text: Exhale and pull the handles back in a wide arc until arms align with shoulders.
With just a slight bend in the arms, pull the handles backward by bringing your arms out to the sides.

claims.text: End point: Motra says stop when the arms line up with the shoulders and avoid going past the torso; Fitness Volt puts the elbows behind the torso. The card follows the more conservative line (arms in line with the shoulders), and Fitness Volt also says to shorten the range if other upper-back muscles take over.

quotes.text: Pull until arms are inline with shoulders; avoid hyperextending past the torso.
Your elbows should be behind your torso at the top.
if you feel greater activation in your other upper back muscles than the rear delts, you should limit your range of motion.

claims.text: Keep the chest on the pad for the whole set. Using momentum is the biggest mistake: having to pull the chest off the pad is a sign of cheating.

quotes.text: Keep your chest in contact with the pad throughout the movement.
If we had to point out the biggest mistake people make while doing the machine reverse fly, it would be their use of momentum.
If you have to pull your chest off the pad at any point during the set, it is a sign you are cheating.

claims.text: Sit upright with a neutral neck, looking straight ahead; a hunched back takes tension off the rear delts.

quotes.text: Maintain an upright torso for the entirety of the set. A hunched back will take tension off your rear delts.
Keep your neck in a neutral position and look straight ahead.

claims.text: Don't go too heavy: heavy loads let the traps dominate, and Fitness Volt (the anchor) says feeling the shoulder blades squeeze together is a sign the weight is too heavy. Motra instead cues squeezing the shoulder blades together at the peak; the card follows Fitness Volt.

quotes.text: Avoid going too heavy to prevent trap dominance
If you feel a scapular retraction, you are probably going too heavy.
Squeeze your rear delts and shoulder blades together at the peak.
Squeeze shoulder blades

claims.text: Stop if you feel sharp pain at the front of the shoulder.

quotes.text: Stop if you feel sharp pain in the front shoulder

claims.text: A neutral grip (palms facing each other) gave more posterior deltoid and infraspinatus activity than an overhand grip on the reverse fly machine (19 trained men, EMG).

quotes.text: The results of this study show that performing exercise on the reverse fly machine with a neutral hand position significantly increases activity of the posterior deltoid and infraspinatus muscles compared with a PRO hand position.

claims.text: The reverse fly machine trains the horizontal shoulder abductors, including the posterior (rear) deltoid.

quotes.text: The reverse fly machine is a popular exercise for strengthening the horizontal shoulder abductors including the posterior deltoid.
The reverse pec deck fly is an isolation exercise that primarily focuses on the posterior deltoids .

claims.text: Pulling the elbows back also works the rhomboids, teres major, infraspinatus and middle trapezius.

quotes.text: Because the machine reverse fly involves pulling your elbows behind your torso, you’ll experience rhomboids, teres major, infraspinatus, and middle trapezius stimulation.

claims.text: Don't let the weight stack rest at the bottom, to keep constant tension.

quotes.text: Do not let the weight stack at the bottom. It will ensure that there is constant tension on your rear delts throughout the set.

claims.text: Tempo: about 1-2 s each way at a moderate speed (ACSM, for heavy sets in trained lifters), with a short squeeze at the back (Fitness Volt suggests a slower 2 s up, 2 s hold, 4 s down).

quotes.text: For intermediate (individuals with approximately 6 months of consistent RT experience) to advanced (individuals with years of RT experience) training
with eventual emphasis on heavy loading (1-6 RM) using 3- to 5-min rest periods between sets performed at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC)
Pause and contract your rear delts for a second before slowly returning to the starting position.
you’ll spend two seconds on the concentric motion, two seconds of contraction at the top, four seconds on the eccentric motion, and no rest at the bottom.

claims.text: Breathe out as you pull the handles back and in as you return.

quotes.text: Exhale as you pull the handles back; inhale as you return to the start.

claims.text: Load progression: add 2-10% load once you can do one or two reps more than the target number.

quotes.text: When training at a specific RM load, it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number.

claims.text: Motra's common-mistakes list for this machine names shrugging the shoulders first.

quotes.text: Shrugging shoulders

claims.text: Tempo: Motra lists 3-1-1 for this lift and its Tempo tooltip gives the order (eccentric, bottom pause, concentric, top pause): 3 s for the return, a 1 s pause at the bottom and 1 s for the pull.

quotes.text: The speed for each phase of the movement, written as four numbers (e.g., 3-1-2-0): eccentric (lowering), bottom pause, concentric (lifting), top pause. Each number represents seconds.

claims.text: Most people go through the motions on this exercise: they overload the machine and rush through the reps; slow down the rep tempo if you can't feel the rear delts working.

quotes.text: While performing this exercise, most people go through the motions for the sake of it. They’ll put more weight on the machine than they can handle and rush through the movement just to achieve their rep target.
You should lower the weights and slow down your rep tempo if you can’t achieve a rear delt pump or at least feel muscle contraction.

plate.viewWhy: Census: front. At the end of the rep the arms are out to the sides in line with the shoulders (c4, c5), which reads clearly from the front. The top fault, pulling the chest off the pad (c6), needs a side view and is left to the posture zoom and text. The shrug (c17) reads from the front too.
plate.equipment: Pec deck set to reverse fly (composed, census R3): seat, chest pad in front of the lifter, two pivot arms with handles at shoulder height (c1, c2). Floor line.
plate.start: Seated upright facing the machine, chest on the pad (c1, c7); arms reaching forward at shoulder height, elbows slightly bent, hands on the handles with a neutral grip (c2, c3, c10).
plate.end: Arms opened out to the sides until in line with the shoulders (c4, c5), elbows still slightly bent (c3), chest still on the pad (c6).

checkpoints.label: Chest on pad
checkpoints.what: The chest stays against the pad for every rep.

checkpoints.label: Soft elbows
checkpoints.what: A slight, fixed bend: not straight, not sharply bent.

checkpoints.label: Stop at shoulders
checkpoints.what: Arms open until in line with the shoulders, not past the torso.

mistake.what: Shoulders shrugged up toward the ears as the arms open.
mistake.why: Fitness Volt's list, the anchor's, puts momentum first (c6); its sign, the chest pulling off the pad, shows only from the side, and the census view is front. Its next item, a slouched back, is also a side-view sign. Motra's list for this machine names "Shrugging shoulders" first (c17); it shows from the front. How often it happens is not measured.
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 1: rushing the reps (c19), R-LB6-5. Fitness Volt's "While performing this exercise, most people go through the motions for the sake of it. They’ll put more weight on the machine than they can handle and rush through the movement just to achieve their rep target." (c19) says most people rush this exercise's reps, a frequency word for a candidate fault of this exercise; the load half is a load and is set aside. No other fault passes step 1. Set aside: Fitness Volt's "The reverse pec deck fly is one of the most popular but incorrectly performed exercises." is about popularity and names no fault; "Here are the most recurrent mistakes people make while performing the reverse pec deck fly:" is a list sentence; "If we had to point out the biggest mistake people make while doing the machine reverse fly, it would be their use of momentum." (c6) ranks by size, not frequency; "While many lifters like to perform the rear peck deck fly as a finisher", "Although most people think rows only target the back" and "they are a lagging muscle group for most lifters" are about programming and muscles; Motra's "commonly scaled by adjusting seat height" is a setting and "Typical Rep Range" programming; StrengthLog's "trains many of the antagonists of common pressing exercises" is about muscles. Rushing shows only as speed, so drawable is false and plate.mistake names the next fault by the same steps. Step 2: no named fault is tied to harm (Fitness Volt's "Lifting too heavy can hamper your form and put you at a greater risk of injury." is the load; Motra's "Stop if you feel sharp pain in the front shoulder", c9, names no fault). Step 3: both lists are written for this exercise, so the anchor's decides: Fitness Volt's "1. Using Momentum", "2. No Mind-Muscle Connection", "3. Slouching Your Back". Momentum's sign, the chest pulled off the pad (c6), is a still sign but shows only from the side, and the census view is front, so it is not drawn either: the mind-muscle item's rushing is already the top fault, the slouched back (c7) is a side-view sign, then Motra's list ("Shrugging shoulders", "Using momentum", "Hyperextending lower back", "Bending elbows too much") gives the shrug first, which shows from the front. Pick changed: plate.mistake moves from the bent elbows (fourth on Motra's list) to the shrug, drawable false; handlingMistakes[0] is now rushing (R-LB6-5) and momentum [1].

tells.text: Arms open level with the shoulders

tempo.text: Up 1 and down 3 are Motra's 3-1-1 (c18, WEAK), whose Tempo tooltip gives the order eccentric (lowering), bottom pause, concentric (lifting), top pause (R-LB6-2); the page shows three numbers, read as the first three, with no top pause. Its 1 s bottom pause sits between the return and the pull, so it is named here and not written in pause (LR-33). Pause 1 is sourced: Fitness Volt's "Pause and contract your rear delts for a second" (c14), right after the pull. Fitness Volt's mistakes section also asks "Pause at the top for a couple of seconds and squeeze the life out of your rear delts." and gives a slower 2:2:4:0 method as a muscle-building variation; the card keeps the how-to step's 1 s and Motra's up and down. Changed from up 2, down 2 (ACSM or a convention) under R-LB6-2.

grip.type: Neutral grip (palms facing each other) preferred; overhand also used.
grip.thumb: Not given by any source read (pull archetype default).
grip.handContact: Not given by any source read (pull archetype default).
grip.wrist: Not given by any source read (pull archetype default).

setup.step: Set the machine's handles to the reverse-fly position.
Set the chest pad and handles so you grip at shoulder height.
Sit facing the machine with your chest pressed against the pad.
Take the handles with a neutral grip, elbows slightly bent.

posture.point: Elbows keep a slight, fixed bend.
Stop when the arms line up with the shoulders.
Don't let the stack rest between reps.

handlingMistakes.fix: Lower the weight and keep your chest on the pad.

rows.means: The rear delts are doing the work.

rows.where: Between the shoulder blades, not shoulders
rows.means: Other upper-back muscles are doing more than the rear delts.
rows.fix: Shorten the range. Stop at the shoulder line.

rows.where: Sharp pain, front of the shoulder
rows.fix: Stop the set. Don't train through the pain.

risks.risk: Sharp pain at the front of the shoulder means stop.
Going too heavy lets the traps take over.

zooms.right: Chest pressed on the pad as the arms open.
zooms.wrong: Chest pulled off the pad to swing the weight back.

zooms.right: Slight, fixed elbow bend as the arms open.
zooms.wrong: Elbows bent sharply as the arms open.

zooms.right: Neutral grip, palms facing each other. Overhand also fine.
